name: Abyssal Razorshrimp
desc: "Our cook could peel a shrimp blindfolded. Said so himself. Someone brought him a black one with a shell like flint, and away he went. Same little fork in the tail after every segment he took off. Soon he had peelings up to his elbows. We cut the blindfold off when he stopped answering. He was peeling his fingers by then, neat as you please."

name: Abyssal Shard Lobster
desc: "Put the slag lobster in the cold locker, says the mate. It took my glove off with the skin inside it. Next morning it lay stiff on the shelf, claws still working. The mate paid me to keep quiet about my hand. I bought a good prosthetic and gave him the lobster for his birthday. Wrapped it up nice. He opened it with his teeth."

name: Abyssal Irisfin
desc: "There's a surgeon's story about an irisfin. She stitched every one of its thousand eyes shut, to get some peace while she ate. Last stitch in, the belly split. All those eyes blinking at her from inside. She threw the thing away and ate her dinner. Admirable woman. I couldn't have managed the soup."

name: Abyssal Gazer
desc: "Don't look into that sideways eye. I did. Saw the poor thing choking, flapping about on the deck. The others swore it hadn't moved. I carried it to the lock, trying to find somewhere it could breathe. They had to break my arm to stop me cycling out with it. Still think about it some nights. Wonder if it's got enough air."

name: Abyssal Necrophyte
desc: "A corpse hauler took a necrophyte aboard and put it in the hold with the dead. Half-rotten fish, smell coming through two sealed hatches. When they went to fetch it out, the oldest corpses had flesh on them again. All stopped at the same stage of rot as the fish. They put it out through the lock. That night somebody in the hold asked them to bring it back."

name: Abyssal Aranea
desc: "We played cards to decide who'd carry the spider-fish down to medical. I lost. Doctor played me double or nothing for taking it to the galley instead. Cook wouldn't play, sensible bastard. The bite left my arm so swollen they had to cut my shirt off. Doctor never did name the venom. Called it 'a gambling injury' and charged me for the shirt."

name: Abyssal Yellowback
desc: "Yellowback looks fit for supper, doesn't it? My aunt caught one and wiped its colour off on a towel. Next wash, all her smalls came out yellow. Then her hands. She swore she hadn't touched the fish again. When her teeth went yellow she threw the lot down the waste chute. Kept her mouth shut in company for years. Couldn't bear anyone asking what she'd done with the towel."

name: Abyssal Rockfish
desc: "My mother used to tell of a hungry sailor who looked through a rockfish's empty belly and saw his own kitchen. His wife was laying supper. He waved, she waved back, and he put his head through to kiss her. 'Was he home then?' I'd ask. Mother always said I could finish the story when I was older. I'm older than she ever got, and I still can't."

name: Abyssal Ghost Manta
desc: "The manta in our song is only a shadow, edges forever coming apart, yet it folds a liner in its wing. Takes the passengers to places they've dreamed of, lets each one off in turn. Last verse is the steward walking the empty decks, setting out breakfast for tomorrow. We used to sing it at launches. My sister booked passage on a liner that never came back, and I can't get through that verse now."

name: Abyssal Ridge Clam
desc: "Two hinges for the living, one for the dead. That's how the old women tell it. A widow opens the ridge clam the wrong way and her husband speaks from inside. She shuts it quick. Spends the rest of the voyage oiling the other two hinges, so he won't hear her taking out the pearls. In my mother's version she asks him where he hid his wages first."

name: Abyssal Nautilus
desc: "Followed a fellow through the docks selling peeps into a nautilus shell. Little dark rooms, each opening on a smaller room, on and on. He said there was a treasure at the bottom. I paid to look twice. Third time he was gone, shell sitting on his stool. Sometimes I wonder whether he found it. Mostly I wonder who took my wallet."

name: Abyssal Eyestar
desc: "Old deck story: lad gets the midnight watch over an eyestar, hundred pupils scattered over five arms. Nothing to do but look at it. He nods off. Wakes with loose pieces all round his chair, wriggling where he can't quite see them. Spends the night staring at each in turn. Come morning, the lad's gone. There's a second chair facing the first, and both seats are warm."

name: Common Crag Crab
desc: "Crab won a race aboard our tug. Against the first mate. He'd wagered a week's pay it couldn't cross the mess before he did. Crab went sideways under the benches; mate tried the same and stuck fast at the shoulders. We counted the crab's legs afterwards, in case it had cheated. All present and proper. Mate stayed there till breakfast."

name: Volturnian Crab
desc: "A captain who'd outlived three crews paid a fortune for a blue crab that was supposed to give him another hundred years. Cracked its glassy shell with a teaspoon and ate the lot. Then he called his officers in, settled their wages and gave the ship to his first mate. Said he'd had enough of living if that was what it cost."

name: Adolescent Pyrcrab
desc: "Cold run, heaters gone, and the engineer's keeping her hands warm on a little fat pyrcrab. Hardly moves, just gets warmer the longer she holds it. By third watch she's got the crew queuing to borrow it. Captain comes down, demands priority. Crab finally bestirs itself and pinches his nose. Engineer gets the heating back by morning. Says she'd have done it sooner if she hadn't been laughing."

name: Adult Pyrcrab
desc: "Never settle an argument about a grown pyrcrab by fetching it for a better look. Our bosun said its legs were on backwards. Carpenter swore it had too many. Cook said the shell was inside out. I carried it between them till it blistered me through the glove. Dropped it straight through the table. They're still arguing. I eat off a crate."

name: Volturnian Lobster
desc: "At a governor's banquet, a cook served blue lobsters he'd hauled from a rupture and charged for the real Volturnian ones. Lovely heavy shells, dreadful meat. Governor called it exquisite. Admiral agreed. Every guest sent compliments to the kitchen. Cook retired on the proceeds. I heard it from his dishwasher, who ate the leftovers and said the governor deserved every mouthful."

name: Rock Lobster
desc: "The oldest lobster story on our boat was about a skipper who couldn't get a plain grey one off his harpoon. Tried every tool aboard. Finally told it, 'Let go and I'll make you captain.' It let go. Crew heard him say it, so they gave the lobster his cabin and put him on galley duty. He cooked it that evening. Nobody would sail with him after."

name: Relic Crab
desc: "A fossil dealer bought a crab off my father. Domed horseshoe shell, long tail spike, all pitted and chipped. Matched a stone cast in his shop, right down to the cracks round the rim. He accused Father of breaking the cast to make a fake. Then the crab crawled off the counter. Dealer doubled his offer. Father took it before either of them could change their mind."

name: Hyperprawn
desc: "Little clear prawns, hundreds in a bucket. We watched them line up and reckoned they were spelling something. Took turns reading letters off to the purser. By dawn he'd filled a whole book. Nobody could agree which way up to hold it. The captain burnt it before we made port. Purser wept like she'd killed his children. Took him three voyages to laugh about it."

name: Steel Pipechovies
desc: "Five pipechovies kept our water running halfway home. Fitted them end to end, dull steel sides, mouths facing the galley. The engineer warned us to run the tap before drinking. I didn't, once. Swallowed something that wriggled all the way down. Been first in the breakfast queue ever since, though I can't rightly say who's hungry."

name: Roider Mudfish
desc: "Roider told me he'd caught a mudfish on an airless rock. I asked where it found the mud. 'Same place I found the fish.' Asked where that was. 'Bottom.' Bottom of what? He looked at me a long while, then bought me a drink. Told everyone in the bar I'd been dropped on my head. They'll still sell you one there if you ask for my name."

name: Berylcuda
desc: "Berylcuda's a ration brick with jaws, my uncle said. Green as bottle glass and about as easy to chew. He used one to break a window during a dockside brawl. Threw it through, climbed after it, broke three teeth falling onto the fish. Swore he'd been bitten. Wouldn't hear a word against it afterwards. Said anything that tough ought to be on his side."

name: Cloudplate Tetra
desc: "An admiral wanted a perfect cloudplate tetra: every little cloud of armour matched on both sides. Sent six ships looking. They brought him hundreds, all wrong. A deckhand finally painted a lopsided one and sold it to him herself. He kept it beside his bed for twenty years. When he died, she bought it back. Says she misses having someone to fool."

name: Tiger Sailfish
desc: "My first skipper wouldn't let a tiger sailfish aboard. Said on his last ship they'd kept one in the mess, its striped fin trailing halfway round the tank. For a fortnight, men dreamed of following that banner out onto the hull. On the fifteenth morning they found the airlock open and half the bunks empty. We threw ours back. He made us sleep in the mess, where he could count us."

name: Silver Slipstreamer
desc: "The silver fish in the pilot's prayer knows a road through every storm. Never slows, never changes heading. A dying navigator asks it to take his last course home, and it does. His ship follows that bright back into port with all hands safe. We used to put a silver scale beneath the nav console. Couldn't hurt."

name: Green Bass
desc: "My father brought home a green bass after every voyage. Mother fried it and asked how far he'd been. 'Farther this time.' When he died we found a tackle bag with one old hook and no line. Mother sat looking at it a while, then said she'd always wondered why his coat smelled of the fish market. She fried the last bass anyway."

name: Jungle Snapper
desc: "The snapper came aboard red and green as a garden bird. Old Deni said there must be a forest out there somewhere, with branches big enough to tie a ship to. He'd spend the dogwatch drawing it for us. Gave every tree a berth number. I kept my drawing. When we've been out too long I like to think somebody's keeping our place."

name: Blue Ochtogon Magifin
desc: "Salvage crew found a fish made of flat blue panels, light shining through the seams. Sold it to a man who swore it was a survey drone. He gave a demonstration in the market, called it to heel, told it to turn. Fish went straight through his stall without changing course. He offered refunds on the spot. A small miracle, round those parts."

name: Blue Tang
desc: "The tang in my grandmother's story carries a scrap of Earth's sky on its back. A homesick sailor asks to borrow it, and the fish lends him enough blue to paint his cabin. Then everyone aboard wants some. By journey's end even the engine room's blue, and the fish hasn't faded a shade. Gran always told that one while she was painting."

name: Soul Bream
desc: "We hauled a soul bream aboard the day our cook died. Broad, plain little thing. Sat in the tank doing nothing while we tried to make his recipes. I said it looked disappointed. Nobody laughed. Next port, the new cook salted his stew and the fish turned over. We buried it with the old man's spoons. That's all I'll say about the name."

name: Venomous Sailfish
desc: "There's a soup-shop story about a beggar who catches a sailfish, all bright warnings and lovely fins. Shopkeeper says he'll cook it for half. Beggar agrees. They quarrel over which half, so the shopkeeper tastes a bit to prove his share's good. Beggar watches him fall down, pockets the till money and goes next door for a meal. Best day's fishing he ever had."

name: Ole' Carp
desc: "Ole' Carp belonged to my ship before I did. Nobody could remember bringing him aboard. Grey old lump, barely shifted when we cleaned his tank. When we sold the ship, the buyer said the fish wasn't included in the inventory. We took him along. Buyer came running down the dock after us, offering another thousand. Claimed the engines wouldn't start. We kept the fish."

name: Credfish
desc: "A man paid his bar bill with a credfish and left town before the landlord looked close. Landlord used it to pay a debt. Passed through six pairs of hands before somebody tried to spend it at the same bar. By then it had a name, a little coat and more credit than the man who caught it. Still couldn't read the number on its side."

name: Long Waller
desc: "A long waller spent a whole voyage feeling under our bunks with its whiskers. Two metres of fish and nowhere to put it. Half the crew fed it scraps; half wanted it gone. When it finally found the bosun's missing boot, with his savings stuffed in the toe, he settled the matter by giving it my bunk. I slept in the passage till port."

name: Eelcat
desc: "There's a wedding custom on one of the old haulers: bride and groom each take an end of an eelcat and promise never to part. Then they spend the reception trying to untangle it from their arms. My cousin and her husband managed in six hours. Her parents are supposed to have taken three days. Twenty years later they're still arguing about who pulled first."

name: Bloody Damsel
desc: "That little orange brute chased three drones all the way into our hold, then tried to evict the loader. We put a mirror by its tank. Fought its own face for a week. I turned the mirror round out of pity. It sulked till I put it back. The bosun said he understood perfectly. He'd been married four times."

name: Goldfish
desc: "We caught a goldfish the day the captain's daughter was born. Came in without a struggle, bright as a new button. He kept it on the bridge all the way home. Couldn't eat it, but some said it brought us luck. The engineer said we'd have got there just as well without it. Captain said that might be so, but he couldn't bring his daughter an engineer in a bowl."

name: Bluefin Theta
desc: "A man dreaming of drowning caught a theta and set it by his bed. Watched it rise and gulp at empty air, over and over, blue fin steady while the rest shook. He began counting its breaths to get to sleep. Helped, he said. Then he started holding his own breath between them. His wife broke the tank. He never forgave her."

name: Adolescent Razorspine
desc: "Razor bets paid my passage when I was young. Grip the little fish behind the head and throw it like a knife. Flies true every time. Last wager was a hundred credits to pin a man's sleeve without drawing blood. I won. He took the fish out with his bare hand and lost two fingers. I gave him the hundred. He wanted the fingers."

name: Hull Grazer
desc: "A tug came in with a hull grazer fastened underneath, big plated head pressed flat, sucking mouth scouring the grit away. Cleanest patch of armour aboard. Skipper asked what he owed for removing it. Yard boss asked what he'd take for leaving it. They bargained all afternoon. Fish let go before they'd settled, and the yard spent the next week trying to catch it with a dirty shuttle."

name: Silver Razorspine
desc: "The smith in the story beats a razor into a fish, gives it a leather belly and throws it at the tax collector. Misses him by a handspan. Fish goes through the floor, through the deck below, clean out the bottom of the station. You can still see the hammer marks on the ones they catch. Tax collector comes back next year with a helmet."

name: Mossy Bass
desc: "We tried growing greens on a mossy bass. Lovely soft stuff along its back, and the fish kept turning it away from the grow lamps. Gardener fussed over it for a month. Harvest supper came round and he served a little salad with every plate. Tasted of damp socks. He ate his own in silence, then asked if anyone wanted seconds. I respected him for that."

name: Largemouth Bass
desc: "Every crew in the docks had caught the biggest bass. We held a contest to settle it. Ours had a crooked jaw; theirs had one fin up by its ear. A third boat brought a fish with a mouth so wide the judge dropped his measure in. Took till evening to get it back. Nobody won. We had a fine supper and held the contest again next year."

name: Moiré Mackerel
desc: "In the prison telling, a warder brings one in for his supper. Its stripes keep sliding about, and the prisoners beg it to move their bars as well. The warder laughs until his eyes hurt from watching the fish. Goes off to lie down. When he wakes, every cell is open. The prisoners took the mackerel with them in the soup pot. Wherever they've got to, they're supposed to feed it first."

name: Marlin
desc: "See that hole above the bar? Marlin. Long as this counter, bill like a boarding pike. We fought it all watch and brought it home to show off. Innkeeper wanted it mounted there. Started measuring while we were still telling him about the fight. Next thing, it was through the wall and into his kitchen. We finished the story outside while he looked for a gun."

name: Pacu Pacu
desc: "My brother swears a pacu smiled at him with our father's teeth. Father was alive at the time, so we went to check. Both had the same chipped incisor. Father wanted to see this for himself. Took one look in the tank and laughed till he cried. Brother never told us what was so funny. Father wouldn't either."

name: Perch
desc: "Striped fish, spines on its back, good in butter. I ate one and went to bed. That's the story. No, I didn't dream anything. Woke up hungry and had another. You can ask the cook. He'll tell you the same, though he'll charge you a drink first. Man's got children to feed."

name: Plume Remora
desc: "The engine-room saint wears remora scales in place of robes. That's how the stokers draw her, blue-white, standing in the drive flame. They say she followed a ship for seven years to fetch her boy home. Didn't feel the heat. Didn't hear them calling. When he finally came down to see what was tapping on the nozzle, she wrapped him up and carried him away."

name: Pomfret
desc: "First fish I caught was a pomfret, silver and broad as a plate. Took no skill at all. I carried it round showing everyone till the cook offered to fry it. Split it six ways so the whole watch could have some. Haven't caught anything since that tasted half so good. Cook says that's because he hasn't let me near his butter again."

name: Pufferfish
desc: "A puffer came aboard so limp the cook thought it was finished. He set it on the counter and went for a pan. Apprentice decided to scare him, put the fish in his pocket and pretended to have lost it. Cook turned round at the screaming. Had to cut the boy out of his trousers. Fish was perfectly all right."

name: Ballooner
desc: "On the old ships they tell of a girl who asks a ballooner to carry a letter to her missing father. Prickly little ball promises it'll try. Trouble is, it can't get through the hatch. Girl cuts it open to let the air out; stays round as ever. So she widens the hatch. That's why the story takes an hour when a shipwright tells it."

name: Deepwater Pufferfish
desc: "That blue one? Used to be no bigger than your thumb. Found a battleship asleep beyond the fabric and puffed itself up until it was twice her size. Frightened her clean out of the dark. My grandfather said that was how the war ended. Couldn't tell me which war. He also said the fish daren't breathe out, in case she comes back."

name: Silver Star
desc: "A pilot lost his wings for drinking and took work hauling fish. One day he caught a silver one that could glide through empty space. Asked it for lessons. Fish taught him well enough to fly home, where his old squadron shot him down for failing to identify himself. That's the squadron version. In his telling he shat on the commander's roof and flew away."

name: Gargantuan Waller
desc: "There was a waller so heavy they had to move it to a fresh cargo bay every morning. Kept getting bigger. At last the crew built a cradle outside and towed it, whiskers trailing behind. By the time they reached port the fish needed a berth and the ship fitted in its mouth. Harbourmaster charged for both. My uncle swore he had the bill."

name: Nemo
desc: "A little orange clownfish came up sealed in a bag. Nobody'd packed it; the bag tested as plasteel. The engineer hung it above her bunk. Said a fish that could arrange its own passage deserved a decent cabin. When she retired she took it with her. Last I heard, it was hanging over a crib. Her grandson thinks all fish come wrapped."

name: Curious Damsel
desc: "We lost a survey drone down a shaft and sent a curious damsel after it. Bright little thing would follow anything with a motor. Came back trailing the drone, two missing probes and somebody's powered chair. We spent a week looking for the chair's owner. Fish kept circling it, waiting for him to switch it on."

name: Flarefin Koi
desc: "A garden keeper had a koi with fins like burning silk. Its light fell on nothing, so he hung lanterns round the pond to see it by. A visitor asked why he bothered keeping such a useless lamp. Gardener pointed at the benches, all full, and asked which of them the visitor wanted him to send away."

name: Stinkfish
desc: "The mutineers never drew a weapon. Put a stinkfish in the captain's cabin and waited. Smell lingered for days after he threw it out. He moved to the bridge. They put another under his chair. Third one went in his escape shuttle before he launched. Cook led the mutiny, they said. He'd been saving them for months."

name: Blue Sea Tuna
desc: "Our pilot reckoned a blue tuna could take us to an ocean. Big fish like that had to be going somewhere. We followed it till fuel ran short, then hauled it in for supper. Pilot refused his share. Said we'd murdered our guide. Cook put his portion in the freezer. He ate it at midnight, with a map open on his knees."

name: Rainbow Carp
desc: "The collector sent us a picture of the carp he wanted. Screens couldn't show half its colours, so we brought him every bright fish we caught. He bought none of them. Then a deckhand dropped the picture into a tank and the water stained it beautifully. Collector paid her for the fish beside it. She told him the colours would fade in transit. He bought the tank as well."

name: Blind Crawler
desc: "Blind crawler found our missing man. Felt its way down the passage, sounding that low note with no water round it. We followed it to a sealed maintenance hatch. Lad was wedged behind the pipes, too weak to shout. After that he wouldn't let anyone eat the fish. Kept it under his bunk. Nobody else slept much, but we let it be."

name: Red Snapper
desc: "Best snapper I ever landed took a piece of my ear. Deep red, teeth like little saws. We fought each other halfway across the deck. Cook won in the end. I asked for my ear back and he said I'd have to wait till he'd cleaned it. Served me the fish himself that evening, with a lemon slice pinned where the ear ought to have been."

name: Coach
desc: "The lad who named the coach had a joke to go with it. Something about taking a ride. Told it at every port, and by the fifth he was getting free drinks to shut up. Tiny silver fish, caught everywhere, so he was asked about it often. Retired rich, according to his daughter. She won't tell the joke for any money."

name: Sulfur Diver
desc: "A salvage crew found a sulphur diver hovering over a hatch in a dead ship. Yellow little thing, stank right through their suits. Wouldn't move. They pulled it clear, and something started hammering on the other side. Let go, fish settled back, hammering stopped. The wreck's still out there, they say. Salvagers leave it alone and bring the fish scraps when they pass."

name: Storm Salmon
desc: "Mother said storm salmon took stray lightning back to the hyperspace clouds. Kept me quiet when the ship shook and the crockery started breaking. Years later, on my first watch in hyperspace, I saw one fighting its way back into the clouds, charge streaming off its tail. Whole convoy was trying to get out. I waved. Couldn't help it."

name: Hammerhead
desc: "A loader put a hammerhead in a torpedo rack by mistake. Blunt casing, tail fins, looked right enough. Gunnery found it when it bit a thumb. They put it in a tank, where it battered the same end till the glass gave. Gunner said they ought to have fired it. Loader said he was welcome to put it back. Neither volunteered to pick it up."

name: Shad
desc: "Caught a shad alone. Thin silver thing, turning with a school we couldn't see. One of the watch said it was keeping place for all the fish we'd eaten. Another said all the sailors we'd buried. Cook said it was keeping place for the potatoes and put it in a pan. We were very young. Spent the whole meal looking at the empty chairs."

name: Silverback
desc: "A silverback jumped clear over our drone and struck the mate square in the chest. Heavy fish, silver down the spine. Broke two ribs. He demanded a rematch as soon as he could stand. We told him there wasn't any surface out there to jump from. Didn't stop the fish, he said. We rigged him a harness and let him make his point."

name: Skate
desc: "My first captain kept a skate. Flat little fellow, sailed over the drones as if they were rocks in a stream. Captain said it was teaching him to fly properly. He'd sit watching it for hours. We thought him soft till we saw him take a damaged freighter through a debris field without touching a plate. I bought a skate when I got my own command."

name: Spined Loach
desc: "A deckhand got a loach's little eye-spine under his thumbnail. Medic pulled it out, cleaned the wound. Weeks later the lad said he could feel whiskers moving inside that finger. Then the next. Begged them to take the hand off. Ship's doctor refused; a dockside surgeon didn't. I saw him years later, both sleeves pinned up. He wouldn't tell me where he felt it now."

name: Ice Tuna
desc: "Ice tuna for the wedding, the bride insisted. Groom broke two reels and a winch bringing one in, frost thick on its flanks. Best meal the station had eaten in years. Bride danced barefoot on the cold deck; groom slept through his own reception. They're still together, last I heard. Every anniversary she lets him choose the menu."

name: Vulcan Cannonfish
desc: "Our gun chief kept a cannonfish beside fire control. Little barrel-bodied brute, looked just like the Vulcans outside. Rattled along with them whenever we were attacked. One watch it started up with nothing on the scopes. Chief woke the gunners anyway. Caught a bomber coming in cold under our bow, cut it apart before it could launch. Captain gave the chief a commendation. He hung it on the tank."

name: Weathervane
desc: "Lost our charts in a fire, so the cook brought a weathervane up to the bridge. Stiff little fish kept pointing the same way however we turned it. Said it would lead us to fishing water. It did. Nearest rupture, every time. We ate well for six weeks before meeting someone who could tell us where the hell we were."

name: Amberjack
desc: "Three months of bass and the crew offered a day's pay apiece for anything else. I hooked an amberjack, yellow tail flashing, and fought it till my shoulders gave out. Passed the gear to the next watch. By the time we landed it, everyone aboard had helped and nobody thought they owed me anything. I charged them for the sauce."

name: Lantern Jack
desc: "Jack carries a dead man's distress beacon on his forehead. Big as a hauler, all mouth beneath the light. You hear the signal better as you close, though the code's decades old. A salvage captain answered once and heard his brother asking for a tow. Brother'd been buried dirtside. Captain went anyway. His crew cut the comms and locked him in his cabin. He still says they left his brother out there."

name: The Quorum
desc: "Ten thousand silver fish came to a king's table, all taken on one hook. He ordered them divided among his guests. Every platter still counted as one fish. Furious, he had the servants count again. Fewer servants came back each time. By midnight the guests were serving themselves, and by dawn the king was laying places for the fish. That's where the little ones learned their manners, my grandmother said."

name: Quorum Splinter
desc: "A dozen fish got left behind when the Quorum ate the king's palace. They keep a place in the middle for whoever's missing. Count them and you get one. My grandmother said a kitchen boy escaped by swimming in that empty place. Asked what became of him. 'Grew up a fish, I expect.' She was washing dishes when she said it. Seemed a perfectly good answer then."

name: Slipstream Moray
desc: "Old Eel sleeps where the fabric's worn thinnest. Slipstreams bend to follow him, and the charts bend with them. A captain decided to measure him by sailing from head to tail. Crew grew old, raised children, taught them the route. Their grandchildren finally reached the end and found their own ship waiting, tied to one of his teeth. Pilot I heard it from said they argued over which crew owed port fees."

name: Shimmerclam
desc: "A miser caught a clam whose shell shone every colour he knew, and some he didn't. Figured the pearl inside would buy a planet. Broke every tool he owned trying to open it. Hired men with better tools. Died owing all of them money, clam still shut. His daughter keeps it on the mantel. Says the outside's pretty enough."

name: Freight Clam
desc: "Check the freight clamps, the loader told his apprentice. Look for the locking lugs. Boy checked every container, found one clam holding a crate of engine parts. Same jaws as a clamp, same lugs round the hinge. He pried it open with his boot. They found the boot still fastened to the crate. Boy told the medic he'd caught his foot in machinery, which was fair enough."

name: Lunacyte
desc: "Took a pale jelly aboard and watched it brighten and dim. No clock matched it. Four of us sat a whole shift trying to count the interval. When we got up, each was sure the others had said something unforgivable. Can't remember what. Haven't spoken to them since. Lunacyte's a good name. Leave it at that."

name: Poison Jelly
desc: "A tanker took a green jelly aboard in an empty drum. Pretty thing. New hand filled the drum with water, thinking he was being kind. By morning it was slurry, and half the mess was sick. The old spacer telling us this wouldn't say whether anyone got home. Just asked who'd have done the same as the new hand. Most of us raised our hands."

name: Aetherial Jelly
desc: "The ghost in the dockside story wears a jelly for a veil. So thin you can hardly see it. Waits on the quay for a sailor who never comes. A child tries to lift the veil and it falls apart in her fingers; the scraps are gone before they touch the ground. Ghost laughs, says she never liked wearing it anyway. After that they wait together."

name: Mussel
desc: "My uncle hid a stolen ring in a mussel. Shell shut tight round something nobody could find, so he reckoned there was room. Customs opened every other bit of cargo and waved him through. He never got the ring back. Ate the mussel with onions, said it was worth the loss. Jeweller didn't agree. Uncle spent a year shucking shellfish to pay him."

name: Deep Terror
desc: "Red octopus escaped its tank every night. Eight arms, could open anything. We put it behind a locked door, then two. Found it in the captain's bath. When a boarding party took our ship, we let them lock us in the hold and waited. Come morning our hatch was open. The captain wouldn't tell us what he found in his bath that time."

name: Yellow King
desc: "The yellow one's got a play written across its hide. I knew a ship where they'd read the first act aloud after supper. Captain forbade the second, so they read it while he slept. By morning he'd locked the whole watch in the brig. They kept rehearsing. New crew could hear them through the deck. Always stopped when somebody went down to listen."

name: Undersea Bee
desc: "A swarm of little jellies followed our tug for a week, each no bigger than a fist. Moved together like parts of something too large to see. Bosun said they were bees and we ought to follow them home for the honey. Captain asked how big he thought the hive would be. Bosun thought a while, then went to check the airlocks."

name: Mind Flayer
desc: "Never saw the squid eat. Got heavier all the same. The man bunking nearest began missing watches, then forgot our names. Doctor wrote meal times on his arm. Soon he couldn't read them. We moved him up to the bridge and threw the squid out. He recovered enough to go home. His wife met us at the dock. He asked me who she was."

name: Crystal Aberration
desc: "A jeweller bought a crystal squid for its colours. Arms cracked and splintered when it moved. She reached into the tank to take a chip and heard the same noise in her wrist. They say she made a fine necklace from what came away. Gave it to her daughter, who keeps it wrapped in cloth. I've seen the cloth. Wouldn't pay to see what's inside."

name: Giant Squid
desc: "The squid inked on the cook. Deep red brute, arms everywhere, got him from boots to collar. We put him in a bucket, bucket in a tub, tub in the washroom. Ink kept spreading. By port the passage was black. Customs wanted to know what we were hiding in there. Cook told them to come and look. They stamped our papers through the hatch."

name: Corona Shark
desc: "A captain brought his lover a shark from the corona, skin bright as a mirror. He'd watched it hunt through the fire without ever catching anything. Far from its star it withered hard as a statue. Lover put it in her garden and married someone else. Captain came back every summer to polish it. Said he was only there to check on the fish."

name: Volley Dolphin
desc: "A volley dolphin kept a crippled shuttle crew alive, so they say. Knocked their drifting marker buoy back whenever it wandered off. Little fellow could hit anything with that nose. By the time rescue came, the pilot had taught it to return a wrench through the broken hatch. They waited another hour to play. Tug captain understood. He'd been alone out there himself."

name: Egg
desc: "There was an egg in the galley when I signed on. Still there when I left. Cook said it would hatch when the last ship came home. Engineer said it'd hatch when the cook learnt to make pastry. Captain said to throw it out before it proved either of them right. It was still there when I signed on again."

name: Bulkhead Turtle
desc: "A yard once built a tug round one of these, mistaking its machined back plates for machinery. Nobody could find the part number under its rear plate in a catalogue, but the foreman wanted the job finished. Tug worked beautifully until the turtle decided to leave. They say it came down the berth on four legs, towing the engines. The crew went after it with a lifting frame."

name: Larva
desc: "When the fish were choosing their shapes, one couldn't decide. Tried fins, tried claws, never finished either. Everyone else went off to sea. It asked a passing sailor what it ought to be. 'Something good in butter,' he said. That's where my father's story ended. Mother used to carry on a bit, give the poor thing another chance."

name: Waterpillar
desc: "A waterpillar crawled past our porthole, rings bunching and stretching against empty space. My little brother thought it was walking on glass. Went from window to window following it. At the last one he asked where it would go when the ship ran out. I said it would manage. He stayed there waving till we couldn't see it anymore."

name: Emmerling
desc: "Emmerling named it after himself. Nobody could find another creature like it in any catalogue, and he wanted to be remembered. He was the cook's assistant on a hauler I knew. Poor lad burnt the breakfast the very next morning. Forty years on, I couldn't tell you the captain's name, but I remember Emmerling. Got his wish, I suppose."

name: Nav Turtle
desc: "A buoy keeper found a turtle holding station where his marker ought to be. Squat shell blinked a perfectly good registration, belonging to no vessel he could find. He left it there and went to lunch. Came back after six months off work and it hadn't shifted an inch. He cleaned the shell, thanked it and asked if it wanted his job permanently. I'm told it still has it."

name: Skelleton
desc: "A surveyor hauled up a fish made entirely of bones and labelled it 'skelleton'. His mate said there was one L too many. They were still arguing when it flapped off the table. Spent the rest of the watch chasing it round the cabin, vertebrae clicking on the deck. Surveyor kept asking what was making it move. His mate told him to shut the bloody door."

name: Banana Star
desc: "Five yellow arms, curved and jointed like fingers. Man who named it banana star had tasted one. Said so proudly in the mess. Medic ran for his kit. We asked how he knew it was worth eating, with venom like that. He said he hadn't known, he'd just missed bananas. He lived. Captain put him ashore somewhere they grew fruit."

name: Crusty Star
desc: "My old ship had a crusty blue star nailed above the galley door. Rough as the plating, never seemed to mind. Captain said it'd been aboard longer than he had. We saluted it when the ship was scrapped. Then the cook pried it loose and took it to his next berth."

name: Crystal Star
desc: "There's a bell aboard a pilgrim ship that nobody is allowed to ring. It's a crystal star, hung on a length of cloth. Once, when the chaplain struck it, something answered from outside. Next watch the answer was closer. The ship visits crowded ports now, and the chaplain won't conduct a service unless the engines are running."

name: Leafy Star
desc: "A starving crew cut an arm from a leafy star and put the rest under a lamp. Grew back before the pot boiled. Fed them all the way home. Captain wanted to sell it; cook refused. In the version I like, he buys the ship and opens a soup kitchen. My brother tells it with a lamp failure, but he's always been a miserable bastard."

name: Scraggly Star
desc: "Scraggly star lost an arm at cards and went looking for a replacement. Borrowed a twig, then a nail, then a finger from a sleeping drunk. Nothing fitted: the gap kept moving to another side. Finally it gave up and learnt to play short-handed. Won its arm back. Lost a different one the following night. Don't gamble with a fish, my aunt used to say."

name: False Dawn
desc: "A salvage crew brought a False Dawn aboard, a little burning jelly their scopes had called a star. Shut it in the spare reactor. Through the inspection glass the chief said he could see his childhood garden. Started waving to someone. They found him with the hatch open, one arm burnt to bone, still waving. The men who dragged him clear left their palms on his shoulders."

name: The Imposter
desc: "My mother waited at the docks every day after my brother's ship went missing. Fifteen years. One morning she saw him waving from a little boat and went aboard before anyone could stop her. Dockmaster said she was laughing. We never found either of them. Boat came back last winter, though. Mum was at the window, waving me over."
